opus-5.5.text:
I think the opportunity is enormous, and it's very much not a winner-take-all situation. When you get a technology this general, it's less like one product and more like a new platform, the way electricity or the internet was. Nobody asks how many companies can succeed with electricity. The answer is basically all of them.

There will be a small number of companies training the largest frontier models, because that takes a staggering amount of compute, capital, and research talent. But that's only one layer. On top of it you'll have companies building products for specific industries like law, medicine, education, and science. You'll have companies building tools, infrastructure, and agents that do real work. And many existing companies will reinvent how they operate. A lot of the value will come from people who deeply understand a particular problem and use these models to solve it far better than was possible before.

The mistake I see is people asking whether the model will get better and make their product irrelevant. If your company exists only because the model is currently bad at something, that's a risky bet. If your company gets much better every time the model improves, you're in a great position. We want to be in the second category ourselves, and we want to help a lot of other companies get there.

So I'm optimistic. I think we'll see an explosion of new companies, some of them very small teams doing what used to take hundreds of people. That will be one of the most exciting parts of the next decade.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI to electricity and the internet, not to the discovery of the transistor.

r002.rationale: It describes AI as a platform used to build products and transform companies, but does not predict that AI will become an unnoticed background component in products.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is going to be one of the biggest platform shifts we've ever seen, maybe the biggest, and in every previous shift like this, the number of companies that got built on top of the new platform was way larger than anyone predicted at the start. When the internet happened, people worried that a few portals would own everything. When mobile happened, people worried Apple and Google would capture all the value. And in both cases, the ecosystem that grew on top was enormous and incredibly diverse.

So my honest view is that there's going to be a small number of companies that build the frontier models, because that's extremely capital intensive and hard, but the value that gets created on top of those models is going to be spread across thousands and thousands of companies. The model is more like electricity or the cloud than it is like a finished product. Intelligence becomes an input, and then the question is who builds the best thing for doctors, for lawyers, for kids learning math, for a particular kind of manufacturing workflow. That's a lot of companies.

The thing I'd tell founders is that the model getting better should feel like a tailwind, not a threat. If your entire company is a thin wrapper that only works because the model has a gap today, you should be nervous, because we're going to close that gap. But if you're building something where a smarter model makes your product better, where you have real users, real data, real distribution, a real understanding of a problem, then every release we ship is good news for you. Those are the companies I'm most excited about, and I think there's room for an unbelievable number of them.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI to earlier platform shifts and models to electricity or the cloud, but does not compare AI’s discovery to the transistor’s discovery.

r002.rationale: Calling intelligence an input and models a platform suggests infrastructure, but the response does not say AI will become an ordinary product component that users do not consciously think about using.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s room for a lot of companies to succeed. It’s tempting to think of AI as one market with one winner, but it’s a technology that can change almost every market. There will be companies building models, companies building infrastructure, and companies creating products that weren’t possible before.

The question is whether you’re doing something people really want. If you can use AI to solve an important problem dramatically better, there’s a huge opportunity. And I don’t think we’ve imagined most of those products yet.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare AI’s discovery to the discovery of the transistor.

r002.rationale: It says AI will enable products across many markets, but does not predict that AI will become an ordinary background component users do not consciously think about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s room for a lot of companies to succeed. It’s tempting to think of AI as one market with one winner, but it’s a technology that can become part of almost everything people do. That creates opportunities at many different levels: building models, building infrastructure, and building products that solve very specific problems.

Having access to a powerful model doesn’t automatically make a great business. You still have to understand what customers need, build something they love, and figure out how to deliver it reliably. There’s a huge amount of work to do there, and I expect a lot of the value will come from companies that find uses we haven’t anticipated yet.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the discovery of AI to the discovery of the transistor.

r002.rationale: It says AI can become part of almost everything people do, but does not communicate that it will be an ordinary background component users do not consciously think about using.
